title: Programmable Probabilistic Computer with 1,000,000 p-bits
abstract: Many problems in physics and machine learning require sampling the collective states of large numbers of interacting variables. On modern graphics processors, repeated movement of interaction data between memory and compute units can limit how efficiently these calculations can scale. Here we demonstrate a programmable probabilistic computer with one million interacting probabilistic bits (p-bits) across 18 field-programmable gate arrays, sustaining $10^{12}$ probabilistic updates per second. Coupling weights remain beside the update circuits in on-chip memory, and only single-bit boundary states pass between devices. Experiments on three-dimensional and quasi-two-dimensional spin glasses show that the ratio of boundary-exchange frequency to local update frequency controls the effect of communication delays on optimization. A bound derived from the graph partition and interconnect identifies operating conditions that recover the residual-energy decay of an unpartitioned GPU reference. Infrequent exchange reduces the decay exponent, although faster local updates can shorten the time to reach a target energy. A cluster mean-field model reproduces this dependence, while ferromagnetic sampling experiments reveal a corresponding dependence of magnetization relaxation on the same frequency ratio. These results establish a million-p-bit computing architecture in which processing and local memory scale together, and provide a quantitative design principle for exploiting tolerance to communication delays in larger probabilistic computers.
